title: Stochastic prefetch efficacy and bank throttling sprint notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick capture of the 2-week spike sprint exploring stochastic prefetch (randomized stride/window) and its interaction with bank-level throttling and eviction behavior under realistic multi-tenant traces. Goal is to decide whether a lightweight randomized prefetcher + adaptive backoff yields net gain vs. current deterministic prefetch and when it harms p99 tails due to bandwidth-induced eviction cascades.

Background / motivation:
- Our current prefetch is conservative deterministic stride-based with fixed window (W=16 pages). It reduces cold page faults but can amplify memory-bandwidth usage and cause eviction storms when many concurrent workers run.
- Observed in customer traces: sudden tail latency spikes when throughput increases (region: us-west2), correlating with NVMe/NVLink channel saturation and elevated eviction rates in KV.
- Hypothesis: introducing stochasticization (randomized window offsets, probabilistic prefetch) smooths simultaneous prefetch waves and reduces synchronized bank pressure. If combined with bank-aware throttling (per-memory-bank token bucket), we can maintain low page-fault rates without saturating bandwidth.

Test/bench setup:
- Machines: p4d-like equivalent hosts (8x A100-sim), 1x NVME per host.
- Workloads: replayed production traces (chat-heavy, seqlen-heavy, mixed-PLG) + synthetic microbench suites to isolate stride patterns.
- Models: bison-3b-like (short context), triage-dl-13b (medium context), longform-70b-reduced (long context emulation via synthetic seqlen).
- Runner: instrumented serving-runtime branch with toggles: PREFETCH_MODE={deterministic,stochastic}, PREFETCH_P=probability per page, PREFETCH_WINDOW=pages, BANK_TOKENS=rate per bank.
- Telemetry: per-request token-count, prefetch-issued, prefetch-hit, page-faults, kv-evictions, memory-bandwidth-sample (per 100ms), tail-latency p50/p95/p99.
- Duration: 30m warmup + 2h run per config.

Key knobs tested (grid):
- PREFETCH_MODE: deterministic vs stochastic
- PREFETCH_P: 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 (for stochastic)
- PREFETCH_WINDOW: 4, 8, 16
- BANK_TOKENS: off, 200MB/s, 500MB/s per bank

Representative results (condensed):
1) Deterministic W=16 baseline (no bank throttling)
   - prefetch-hit 68% overall, page-faults ↓ 45% vs no-prefetch
   - memory bandwidth avg ↑ 28%, p99 latency +12ms under 80% load
   - eviction rate +34% during 75-90th minute multi-tenant surge

2) Stochastic P=0.5 W=8, no bank throttling
   - prefetch-hit 59% (expected drop), page-faults ↓ 32%
   - memory bandwidth avg ↑ 18% (lower than deterministic)
   - p99 tail improved vs baseline by ~3ms during surge (less synchronized waves)
   - eviction rate +18% (better than baseline)

3) Stochastic P=0.5 W=8 + BANK_TOKENS=200MB/s
   - prefetch-hit 55%, page-faults ↓ 28%
   - memory bandwidth avg constrained, peak bursts clipped
   - p99 tail improved by 10ms vs deterministic baseline; p99.9 still has rare spikes tied to background NVMe GC
   - eviction rate +9% (good improvement), fewer subsequent cold faults

4) Stochastic P=0.8 W=16 + BANK_TOKENS=200MB/s
   - behaves similarly to deterministic window but with slightly smoothed bursts
   - bandwidth still high -> when background NVMe latency increases (simulated GC) we see backpressure and p99 regressions

Micro-observations from trace correlation:
- Prefetch waves align with request arrival bursts for deterministic case (clear vertical stripes in heatmap). Stochastic spreads these stripes horizontally which reduces instantaneous bank concurrency.
- Evictions measured tend to be short-lived cascades: a sudden prefetch flood will evict pages, causing near-immediate cold faults for other requests, which in turn triggers more prefetches and a small positive feedback loop. Smoothing the prefetch reduces the feedback amplitude.
- Bank token bucket is effective at clipping prefetch-generated bursts but must be tuned by workload; too strict -> increases page-faults and latency; too loose -> ineffective. Adaptive target should be set to maintain ~70% of observed healthy-bandwidth.

Quantitative sanity-checks / anomalies:
- In one mid-run (P=0.5,W=8) we saw prefetch-hit drop to 31% for 3 minutes — traced to an unrelated background job that primed the NVMe and pushed out resident pages. Lesson: need to correlate control-plane maintenance jobs in telemetry and exclude them for SLA calculations.
- Under long-context synthetic (many KV pages sequentially hot), prefetch provided superlinear benefit (page-faults down 61%) because sequential locality amplified hits. This suggests adaptive mode that increases P and W when longer-run locales are detected.

Profiling notes (how we measured)
- Kernel: captured page-fault histograms via /proc and our runtime counters.
- GPU-host link: nvlink counters and nvidia-smi sampling (10Hz) for bandwidth footprint.
- NVMe latency: perf + iostat; we also recorded SMART counters to catch ephemeral GC periods.
- Custom instrumentation: added metrics prefetch.issued, prefetch.cancelled, bank.throttled_ms per bank.

Design implications / recommended direction:
1) Implement a hybrid prefetcher:
   - Default stochastic prefetch with dynamic P tuned from recent page-fault rate and bank headroom.
   - Locality detector: if sequential locality > threshold, temporarily boost P and W until reuse drops.
2) Bank-aware backoff controller:
   - Token-bucket per-bank with feedback loop reading bandwidth headroom from telemetry every 1s.
   - Backoff policy: reduce P by 20% when bank utilization > 85% for >500ms, restore gradually.
3) Eviction-aware prefetch cancellation:
   - If prefetch would evict a page with reuse_score > X (recently accessed by active requests), cancel prefetch or lower priority.
   - Need inexpensive reuse_score heuristics (LRU-time-since-last or bloom filter).

Short to medium-term action items (owners):
- (Maya) Prodize stochastic prefetch flag behind FF, add metrics, and rollout to canary 5% traffic (INF-1723). Target: next sprint.
- (Ethan) Implement bank token-bucket library and expose bank-level telemetry (GH PR linked). Add unit tests for token replenishment corner cases.
- (Priya) Build locality detector prototype (LRU-window based) and integrate with prefetcher for adaptive boost.
- (Liam) Create dashboard widgets showing prefetch vs eviction correlation, and add alert when eviction rate delta > 10% baseline post-rollout.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How to set initial conservative defaults for BANK_TOKENS across heterogeneous instances (PCIe vs NVLink)? Need a micro-benchmark matrix by instance type and provider.
- Should prefetches be prioritized lower than live request IO to avoid creating cold-request starvation? (initial tests show yes, but edge cases remain)
- What telemetry volume is acceptable for production (per-page signals are noisy)? We need to aggregate smartly to avoid observability cost.

Notes to self / rough checklist for canary rollout:
- Ensure FF toggle exists and is safe to flip per-serving-pool.
- Add prefetch and bank metrics to per-pool retention (24h fast, 7d slow).
- Add a kill-switch at routing level that disables prefetch globally if p99 increases beyond threshold.
- Prepare runbook snippets: how to throttle BANK_TOKENS from console.

Appendix: raw numbers (select run)
- Deterministic W=16: avg BW 4.8GB/s, burst peak 7.1GB/s, eviction rate 0.34 (evictions/sec/1000reqs)
- Stochastic P=0.5 W=8 + tokens200: avg BW 3.9GB/s, peak 4.6GB/s, eviction rate 0.09
- Cold faults per minute: baseline 7.2 -> stochastic+bank 2.9

Conclusion:
Stochastic prefetch combined with light bank-level throttling meaningfully reduces synchronized bandwidth bursts and downstream eviction cascades for multi-tenant traces. The tradeoff is slightly lower prefetch-hit and modestly higher cold faults in isolated cases, but overall p99 improves when throttling is applied. Recommend moving forward with a hybrid implementation (stochastic default + locality-triggered boost + bank-aware backoff) and canary rollout with the metrics/alerts described.

End of sprint notes.
